documents.title: Maritime CFD and Naval Architecture
documents.content: Maritime engineering at SandebTech covers simulation-driven design and optimization of ships, propulsors and offshore structures. Using CFD together with parametric geometry, vessels are optimized to decrease fuel consumption, reduce operational downtime and maximize speed. Typical work spans hull form development, propeller design, appendage and energy saving device optimization, seakeeping and offshore structure analysis.

documents.title: Ship Hull Form Optimization
documents.content: Hull form optimization uses fully parametric hull models combined with CFD to minimize calm-water resistance and improve propulsive efficiency. Workflows create either a fully parametric hull from scratch or apply morphing to an imported hull, then run automated design variations. Typical targets include wave-making resistance, wetted surface area, bulbous bow shape, forebody and aft body refinement, and wake field quality into the propeller plane. Geometric, stability and arrangement constraints are respected automatically so every variant remains buildable.

documents.title: Propeller Design and Optimization
documents.content: Propeller optimization covers fully parametric blade geometry generation and CFD driven performance evaluation. Supported propulsor types include conventional fixed pitch, tip rake, variable pitch, outboard and surface piercing propellers. Objectives typically balance open water efficiency, thrust delivery, cavitation margin and pressure pulse levels on the hull. Because the propeller is optimized in the wake of the actual hull, interaction effects are captured rather than assumed.

documents.title: Resistance Reduction and Fuel Efficiency
documents.content: Resistance reduction studies predict the speed-resistance and speed-power curves that drive vessel operating cost. Total resistance is decomposed into frictional, wave-making and form components so effort is spent where the gain is. Typical energy savings of around five percent are achievable through systematic hull and appendage optimization. Results feed directly into EEDI and EEXI compliance work and into realistic fuel and emissions projections.

documents.title: Energy Saving Devices (ESD)
documents.content: Energy Saving Devices recover otherwise lost rotational and wake energy around the propeller. SandebTech designs and optimizes pre-swirl ducts and stators, wake equalizing ducts, rudder bulbs and fins, and pre/post swirl arrangements. Because ESD performance depends entirely on the local flow field, devices are optimized in the coupled hull-propeller-rudder system rather than in isolation. ESDs are attractive for both newbuild designs and retrofit programmes where hull changes are not possible.

documents.title: Seakeeping and Added Resistance in Waves
documents.content: Seakeeping analysis evaluates vessel behaviour in realistic sea states rather than calm water alone. Simulations predict ship motions in regular and irregular waves, response amplitude operators, added resistance in waves, sinkage and trim. Outputs support operability assessment, crew and passenger comfort criteria, slamming and green water risk, and the weather factor required for EEDI calculations.

documents.title: Offshore Structures and Platforms
documents.content: Offshore work covers floating and fixed structures including FPSOs, semi-submersibles, spars, and offshore wind and tidal energy installations. Analysis addresses current and wave loading, motion response, station keeping and mooring behaviour, and local flow around risers and appendages. Parametric modelling allows early-stage exploration of hull column and pontoon arrangements before detailed engineering begins.

documents.title: Yacht and High Speed Craft Design
documents.content: Yacht and high speed craft design covers America's Cup class hulls and foils, catamarans with superstructure, planing motor boats and fast patrol craft. Planing hulls require attention to dynamic trim, running attitude and spray, while sailing yachts additionally involve appendage and sail interaction. Parametric modelling supports rapid early-stage exploration where a large number of variants must be assessed quickly.

documents.title: Wind Assisted Ship Propulsion
documents.content: Wind Assisted Ship Propulsion adds thrust from Flettner rotors, wing sails or suction sails to reduce fuel burn on conventional vessels. Simulation addresses aerodynamic thrust and side force generation, interaction between multiple devices and the superstructure, induced heel and leeway, and the resulting change in rudder and propeller loading. Placement and sizing studies are run parametrically across realistic wind roses for the intended trade route.

documents.title: SHIPFLOW Solver Technology
documents.content: SHIPFLOW from FLOWTECH is a CFD system built specifically for ship hydrodynamics rather than a general purpose code. It uses a zonal approach: XPAN is a potential flow panel method that predicts waves and wave resistance rapidly with accuracy sufficient for hull ranking, XBOUND handles boundary layer effects, and XCHAP is the viscous RANS solver used for double model and free surface computations. SHIPFLOW MOTIONS is a time accurate non-linear boundary element method for ship motions and added resistance. Grids are generated automatically from the hull shape, and an overlapping grid technique handles appendages.

documents.title: CAESES for Maritime Geometry and Optimization
documents.content: CAESES provides the parametric geometry and optimization layer for maritime projects. Fully parametric hull, appendage and propulsor geometries can be built from scratch, or imported geometry can be modified rapidly with advanced morphing techniques. Robust variants are generated with minimal failures while geometric, stability and arrangement constraints are respected automatically. Geometries export in multiple CFD-ready formats, and integrated DoE, optimization algorithms and post-processing close the loop with external solvers such as SHIPFLOW.

documents.title: Benefits of Maritime Simulation
documents.content: Simulation driven maritime design delivers measurable value: typical energy savings around five percent from systematic hull and appendage optimization, thousands of design variants explored instead of a handful, full constraint consideration so results remain feasible, and far fewer physical model tests. Design decisions move earlier in the programme where change is cheap, and regulatory targets such as EEDI and EEXI can be addressed proactively rather than retroactively.

documents.title: Maritime and Naval Architecture Terminology
documents.content: Common terms: Block coefficient (Cb) is the ratio of displaced volume to the enclosing box, indicating hull fullness. Froude number scales wave-making behaviour. Reynolds number scales viscous behaviour. LCB is the longitudinal centre of buoyancy. Wake fraction describes the slowed flow the propeller actually sees. Thrust deduction accounts for the extra resistance the working propeller induces on the hull. Form factor relates viscous resistance to flat plate friction. EEDI and EEXI are IMO efficiency indices for new and existing ships. RAO is a response amplitude operator relating wave input to motion output.

documents.title: How accurate is marine CFD compared to towing tank tests?
documents.content: Modern marine CFD is routinely validated against towing tank and sea trial data. Resistance predictions for conventional displacement hulls typically correlate within a few percent when best practice grids and turbulence models are used. CFD does not replace physical testing entirely; the usual approach is to use CFD to rank and optimize many variants early, then verify the final one or two candidates in the tank. This is faster and cheaper than testing many physical models.

documents.title: How long does a hull optimization project take?
documents.content: Project duration depends on scope. A focused resistance study on an existing hull is typically a matter of days. A full parametric hull optimization with hundreds of variants, appendages and self-propulsion assessment usually runs over several weeks. Because the parametric model is reusable, follow-on studies on the same vessel family are considerably faster. Contact SandebTech with your vessel type and objectives for a specific schedule.

documents.title: What data is needed to start a maritime CFD project?
phrases: what do i need to provide
documents.content: A typical maritime CFD project starts from the hull geometry in IGES, STEP or a surface mesh format, or a table of offsets. Also useful are the loading conditions and hydrostatics, design and operating speed range, propeller particulars if available, and any appendage arrangement. If a parametric model is required, existing lines plans are sufficient as a starting point for fitting. Where geometry is confidential, work can proceed under NDA.
